Industrial emissions in coastal regions have risen by forty-three percent over the past decade, yet our domestic carbon pricing mechanisms fail to account for imported goods with massive embedded emissions. We impose constraints on our farmers and manufacturers while welcoming products made under far looser environmental standards abroad. This is not environmental leadership. It is economic self-harm disguised as virtue. The data from our own Environmental Protection Agency confirms what local businesses have been telling me for months. Small and medium enterprises face regulatory costs that their international competitors simply do not bear. A manufacturer in Cork pays carbon taxes while competing against subsidised goods from countries with no meaningful emissions controls whatsoever. The playing field is not merely uneven, it is fundamentally broken. What we need is border carbon adjustment mechanisms that reflect the true environmental cost of production. If we are serious about reducing global emissions, we must ensure that goods entering our market meet comparable standards. Otherwise, we are simply exporting emissions and jobs simultaneously. The Government speaks eloquently about climate justice, but justice requires consistency. You cannot penalise domestic producers while rewarding foreign polluters with market access. The agricultural sector faces similar contradictions. Our farmers are told to reduce methane output while we import beef from regions actively engaged in deforestation. The hypocrisy is staggering. Irish agriculture represents some of the most sustainable food production in the world, yet Government policy treats it as a problem to be managed rather than an asset to be supported.

This represents over five billion dollars in investment and will create thousands of high-quality jobs in a sector that is absolutely critical to our economic future. It demonstrates what we can achieve when different levels of government work together with industry partners and labour organisations toward a common goal. The member opposite characterises our approach in negative terms, but let me provide some facts. Canada has attracted more investment in the electric vehicle supply chain over the past two years than in the previous two decades combined. We are building a competitive advantage in battery manufacturing, critical mineral processing, and vehicle assembly that will position our workers and our communities for long-term prosperity. This is not happening by accident. It is the result of deliberate policy choices, strategic investments, and partnership building. The transition to clean technology represents the greatest economic opportunity of our generation. Countries that move first will capture the jobs and the growth. Those that hesitate will find themselves dependent on foreign supply chains and foreign technology. We have chosen to lead. The Inflation Reduction Act in the United States has spurred unprecedented competition for investment in this sector. Our response has been to ensure that Canada remains an attractive destination by matching incentives, reducing regulatory barriers, and investing in the infrastructure that these projects require. The opposition would have us sit on the sidelines while other jurisdictions secure the investments and the jobs. That is not leadership. That is abdication.

the mental health of students. The examinations matter, credentials matter, but young people matter more. We have consulted extensively with educators, with parents, with the students themselves. The message has been consistent. They want clarity, they want fairness, and they want to know that their wellbeing is at the centre of any decision we make. I want to be absolutely clear about the timeline. The examinations are postponed, not cancelled. We are working to identify dates that provide sufficient preparation time while minimising disruption to the academic calendar. The State Examinations Commission is modelling several scenarios, and we expect to announce final dates within the next fortnight. What we will not do is rush students into examination halls when they have not had adequate time to prepare or when public health conditions make it inadvisable. Alternative assessment mechanisms are also under consideration. We learned valuable lessons during the previous disruption about predicted grades, their strengths and their limitations. Any system we implement must command public confidence. It must be fair to students regardless of their school or their background. Educational equity cannot be an afterthought. It must be the foundation of whatever approach we ultimately adopt. I have spoken with principals who report significant variation in student readiness depending on how severely their schools were affected by the closures. Some students have maintained access to quality remote learning. Others have not. We cannot ignore that reality when designing assessment systems.

and reconciliation processes in areas affected by conflict. Faith communities often have established trust and relationships that span divides which governments and international organisations struggle to bridge. They can convene conversations that would otherwise be impossible. They provide neutral spaces where adversaries can meet without losing face. The evidence demonstrates that locally-led peacebuilding initiatives have significantly higher success rates than externally imposed frameworks. When churches and faith-based organisations engage in this work, they bring not only logistical capacity but also moral authority that resonates within the communities they serve. They understand the cultural context. They speak the language, both literally and figuratively. They remain present after international attention moves elsewhere. Our funding priorities must reflect this reality. The Department has committed additional resources to support grassroots peacebuilding efforts, but we must ensure those resources reach the organisations doing the actual work on the ground. Too often, funding is consumed by intermediaries and administrative overhead. Direct support to local faith-based organisations represents better value and better outcomes. I want to emphasise that supporting faith-based peacebuilding does not mean favouring one religion over another or imposing religious frameworks on secular communities. It means recognising that in many conflict-affected areas, religious identity is central to how people understand themselves and their relationships. Ignoring that reality in the name of secularism would be counterproductive.

Yet remarkably, Mr. Hallett has attracted a following of individuals who accept his narrative and have involved themselves in various activities premised on this fiction. Some have suffered financial harm as a result. Some have become estranged from their families. The situation has evolved from eccentric delusion into something more concerning. Local authorities report increasing incidents involving individuals claiming sovereign citizen status based on Mr. Hallett's assertions. They refuse to recognise the legitimacy of our courts, our taxes, our regulatory frameworks. They cite elaborate legal theories that have no basis in actual law. When challenged, they become hostile and occasionally threatening. This presents real challenges for police, for council officers, for anyone attempting to enforce legitimate authority. I want to be clear that Mr. Hallett has every right to hold and express his views, however divorced from reality they may be. Free speech protects even absurd claims. What it does not protect is fraud, harassment, or incitement to lawlessness. Where his activities or those of his followers cross that line, enforcement action must follow. The challenge is that much of what occurs exists in a grey area where the conduct is disruptive but not clearly criminal. The broader question this case raises concerns our collective resilience against misinformation and conspiracy theories. When individuals can attract significant followings making claims that are trivially disprovable, we must ask what social and psychological needs are being met by these narratives.

Reconciliation cannot be a talking point deployed when politically convenient and ignored when difficult choices arise. It must be the foundation of our relationship with Indigenous peoples, tested and proven through decisions on land rights, on resource development, on service delivery, on all the practical matters that affect daily life. The member for Kenora is absolutely right to challenge us on this. When we use the language of nation-to-nation relationships, we must be prepared to accept what that actually means. It means recognising inherent rights. It means consulting not as a courtesy but as a requirement. It means accepting that Indigenous communities have the authority to say no, and that our role is to work within that reality rather than around it. Too often, consultation becomes a box-ticking exercise designed to legitimise decisions already made. This bill represents progress, and I support it. But we should not congratulate ourselves too enthusiastically for doing what should have been done decades ago. The standard we should set is not whether legislation is better than nothing, but whether it meaningfully addresses the gaps and injustices that persist. By that measure, we still have considerable work ahead. I want to speak specifically to the economic dimensions of reconciliation. Indigenous communities have been systematically excluded from economic opportunities on their own territories for generations.

They see crime rising. They see streets that are no longer cleaned properly. They see youth services that have been cut. They see libraries operating reduced hours. These are not abstract policy debates. These are material realities that diminish quality of life and opportunity. The Government will argue that tough choices had to be made in difficult fiscal circumstances. But choices reveal priorities, and this Government's priorities are clear. Tax cuts for those who need them least. Austerity for everyone else. The distributional analysis shows exactly who benefits and who pays. Wealthier households receive substantial net gains. Working families and those on fixed incomes see their real disposable income decline. The Government calls this fairness. The dictionary calls it something else. Local government has been particularly hard hit. Councils are expected to deliver more services with fewer resources. They are criticised when services deteriorate, but given no means to address the underlying funding gap. The promise of devolution rings hollow when it means devolving responsibility without devolving resources or authority. Central government retains control over revenue-raising powers while downloading costs and blame onto local authorities. This Finance Bill perpetuates that dysfunctional model. It offers no pathway toward sustainable local government finance.

This is critical infrastructure that should have been built years ago. The existing system is fragile. A single burst main can leave thousands of households without water for extended periods. That is not acceptable in a modern European country. The broader question this project raises is why we have systematically underinvested in water infrastructure for decades. We are now playing catch-up, spending more money to fix problems that could have been prevented with proper maintenance and timely upgrades. The penny-wise, pound-foolish approach to infrastructure investment costs us all in the long run. Burst mains waste water. Service interruptions disrupt businesses and households. Boil water notices undermine public health. Irish Water has come under considerable criticism, some deserved and some not. The organisation inherited a system that was neglected for generations. Fixing that requires time and money. The question is whether we are prepared to provide both. Public patience is understandably thin when they see bills rising while service quality remains poor. But the alternative to investing now is accepting continued deterioration. The Windmill Hill project is part of a broader plan to modernise water supply across the region. I have reviewed the full scheme, and it represents a reasonable approach given the constraints.

They involve individuals who operated in high-stress environments, who made split-second decisions with life-or-death consequences, and who now face prosecution years after the fact based on evolving legal standards. The challenge we face is balancing the rights of victims with the unique circumstances of military and police service. Victims deserve justice. They deserve to be heard. They deserve to see those who harmed them held accountable. But justice also requires context. It requires understanding the difference between malicious criminal conduct and tragic mistakes made under extreme pressure. Our legal system should be capable of making those distinctions. What troubles me most is the sense among serving members that the government will not stand behind them when controversies arise. They are asked to put themselves in danger, to make difficult decisions, to carry out missions that the rest of us are grateful we never have to perform. In return, they deserve our support. That does not mean immunity from accountability. It means fair process, recognition of context, and acknowledgment that we ask them to operate in circumstances where perfect decisions are impossible. The McClintic case illustrates this failure vividly. Policy decisions were made that prioritised the comfort of an offender over public safety and the healing of victims' families.

Local stakeholders report frustration with the lack of clear direction from government departments. What was once a promising initiative now feels stuck in administrative limbo. This is a familiar pattern. Governments announce ambitious projects with great fanfare. Press releases are issued. Photo opportunities are arranged. Ministers speak eloquently about transformation and innovation. Then the hard work begins, and momentum dissipates. The organisations expected to deliver the project find themselves navigating contradictory requirements, uncertain timelines, and inadequate resources. Eventually, the project is quietly shelved or reduced to a pale shadow of what was originally promised. South Wales cannot afford another false start. The region has experienced decades of economic disruption following the decline of traditional industries. People there have been promised regeneration repeatedly. They have learned to be skeptical. Delivering this environmental technology project would demonstrate that government commitments actually mean something. Failing to deliver would confirm the cynicism that already exists. What I want from the Minister is clarity. Is this project proceeding or not? If it is proceeding, what is the timeline? What are the specific obstacles, and what is being done to address them. If it is not proceeding, the Minister should say so honestly rather than allowing uncertainty to continue.

fact, they are often the level of government closest to the lived experience of ordinary people. They manage services that affect daily life. They respond to local priorities. They understand community needs in ways that central government cannot. Yet for too long, they have been treated as administrative extensions of central authority rather than democratic institutions in their own right. This Bill represents a welcome shift in that relationship. By strengthening local authority powers and responsibilities, we acknowledge that good governance requires genuine local democracy. It requires elected representatives who are accountable to the communities they serve and who have the resources and authority to make meaningful decisions. The challenge will be implementation. Empowering local authorities on paper is easy. Ensuring they have the fiscal capacity, the administrative capability, and the political space to exercise that power is harder. Central government has a habit of granting authority while withholding resources. Devolution becomes a way of downloading blame without genuinely redistributing power. If this Bill is to achieve its objectives, it must be accompanied by real financial reform. Local government financing in this country is badly broken. Councils depend heavily on central grants, which makes them vulnerable to budgetary pressures and political manipulation. They have limited revenue-raising authority, which constrains their ability to respond to local priorities. The result is a system where local representatives are held accountable for decisions they did not make and outcomes they cannot control.

The key point is ensuring that the arbitration process operates fairly and efficiently. When arbitrators fail to meet the standards required, there must be mechanisms to address that. The Bill provides those mechanisms. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors raised concerns about the specific grounds for removal and whether they were sufficiently clear. We listened to those concerns. We worked with the organisation to refine the language. The result is a framework that protects the integrity of the arbitration process while also providing appropriate safeguards for arbitrators themselves. Arbitration serves an important function in resolving disputes without resorting to costly and time-consuming court proceedings. But arbitration only works when both parties have confidence in the process. That requires competent arbitrators operating under clear rules. It also requires mechanisms to address situations where arbitrators are conflicted, incompetent, or otherwise unable to fulfill their duties properly. The Bill strikes the right balance. It provides clear grounds for removal where necessary while also ensuring that arbitrators are not removed arbitrarily or for improper reasons. The consultation process with stakeholders has been extensive. We received feedback from legal professionals, from industry bodies, from those who regularly use arbitration services. That feedback has been carefully considered and, where appropriate, incorporated into the Bill. The result is legislation that commands broad support across the sectors it affects. I want to thank the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors and other stakeholders for their constructive engagement throughout this process. Their expertise has improved the Bill.

The infrastructure exists. The connectivity exists. What we need is strategic investment and policy support to unlock that potential. I was encouraged by the Tánaiste's visit and by the commitment shown to the future mobility hub. This facility could transform Shannon into a genuine multimodal logistics centre. It could attract investment. It could create jobs. It could position the mid-west as a competitive location for companies looking at European distribution. But potential means nothing without follow-through. We have seen too many promises made to regional Ireland that were never delivered. The mid-west has particular reason to be skeptical given past disappointments. What we need now is action. We need firm timelines. We need committed funding. We need government departments working collaboratively rather than in silos. The mobility hub project involves multiple agencies and multiple government departments. Coordination is essential. So is accountability. Someone needs to be responsible for driving this forward and ensuring that progress happens. I would also note that Shannon's potential extends beyond cargo. The airport has been a vital piece of infrastructure for the region for decades. It supports tourism. It supports business connectivity. It supports the regional economy in ways that are sometimes underappreciated. We must ensure that Shannon continues to have the runway capacity, the facilities, and the route network to serve those functions effectively.

It enables rapid response when safety issues are identified. It provides data that can inform clinical practice and guide future device development. Transparency is essential. Patients and healthcare providers need access to information about device safety and performance. The information system will make that possible. But transparency must be balanced with privacy. Patient data must be protected. Commercial confidentiality must be respected where legitimate. The challenge is designing systems that serve all these purposes simultaneously. The technical specifications for the information system are still being developed. We are consulting with clinical experts, with device manufacturers, with patient groups, with data protection authorities. Getting this right requires input from all those perspectives. We cannot design an information system that serves regulatory purposes but is too cumbersome for clinical use. We cannot create transparency requirements that discourage innovation or impose unreasonable costs on small manufacturers. The system must be proportionate. It must be practical. It must actually improve patient safety rather than simply generating paperwork. Subsection five provides the flexibility to develop requirements that meet those objectives. It sets the framework without prescribing every detail in primary legislation. That allows for adaptation as technology evolves and as we learn from experience. I believe that is the right approach given the complexity of the issues involved.

The people of Cork, Limerick, Waterford, and Galway deserve to know when they will have the opportunity to decide on directly elected mayors for their cities. I understand there are complex questions about powers, about budgets, about the relationship between directly elected mayors and city councils. Those questions need to be resolved. He believes that Western expansion into that sphere represents aggression against Russia. He rejects the principle that those countries have the sovereign right to choose their own alliances and their own futures. This is not new behaviour. We have seen it in Georgia. We have seen it in Crimea. We have seen it in eastern Ukraine. We have seen it in Syria. The pattern is clear. Putin uses military force to pursue political objectives when he believes he can do so without facing unacceptable costs. The question for the West is how to impose those costs. Economic sanctions are one tool. Military support for countries defending themselves is another. Diplomatic isolation is a third. All have roles to play. But we must be realistic about what they can achieve and how long that will take. Putin is not going to wake up one day and decide that respecting the sovereignty of neighbouring countries is in Russia's interest. Change will come through sustained pressure, through the erosion of domestic support as the costs of his policies become apparent, through the eventual recognition that Russia's long-term prosperity requires integration with the global economy rather than confrontation with it. That is a long-term project. It requires patience and resolve. It requires maintaining Western unity even as the immediate crisis fades from headlines. The House must understand that we are in this for the duration.

self-employment. The current system creates perverse incentives. It encourages the misclassification of workers as self-employed when they should properly be classified as employees. This benefits employers by reducing their tax and National Insurance obligations. It harms workers by denying them employment rights and protections. It costs the Treasury revenue. Everybody loses except the employers engaging in these practices. The Labour Party's proposal for statutory definitions of employment status would address this. It would provide clarity. It would reduce the scope for manipulation. It would ensure that workers are classified based on the reality of their working relationship rather than the label attached to their contract. The Taylor review recognised this problem and made sensible recommendations. The Government has dragged its feet on implementation. Meanwhile, the problem grows worse. More workers find themselves trapped in bogus self-employment. More employers undercut competitors by avoiding obligations that legitimate businesses meet. More revenue is lost to the Exchequer. The time for action is long overdue. We need clear statutory definitions. We need robust enforcement. We need penalties for employers who deliberately misclassify workers. The technology platforms have received particular attention, and rightly so. But the problem extends far beyond the gig economy. It affects construction, it affects care work, it affects logistics, it affects numerous sectors. A comprehensive solution must address all of them. That is what Labour is committed to delivering.

Skills training, employment programs, post-secondary education support, housing initiatives targeted at first-time buyers. The list goes on. The member characterises this as inadequate, but perhaps he could explain what he would do differently. Would he spend more. If so, how would he pay for it. Would he target the spending differently. What young Canadians need is not political rhetoric but practical support that helps them build successful lives. They need access to education and training that prepares them for the jobs of tomorrow. They need opportunities to enter the workforce and develop their careers. They need housing they can afford. They need to believe that their future will be better than their present. This government is delivering on all those fronts. Are there young Canadians still struggling. Of course there are. Is more work needed. Of course it is. But the suggestion that this government is indifferent to the challenges facing young people is absurd. The budget figures speak for themselves. The programs we have implemented speak for themselves. The outcomes we are achieving speak for themselves. I would welcome constructive suggestions from the member opposite about how we can do even better. What I will not accept is baseless criticism that ignores the substantial progress we have made.

our commitment must be unwavering despite the challenges we face. The situation requires immediate attention from multiple government departments working in coordination. Resources must be allocated efficiently and transparently. Local communities affected by these decisions deserve clear communication about timelines and expected outcomes. We cannot afford delays that compound existing problems. The constituents I represent have made their views abundantly clear through correspondence and public meetings. They expect action, not excuses. They expect accountability, not bureaucratic deflection. This House must respond to those legitimate expectations with concrete measures. I have reviewed the relevant departmental briefings and consulted with experts in the field. The technical aspects are complex but manageable with proper planning. What we need is political will to drive implementation forward. Previous attempts have faltered due to inadequate coordination and insufficient follow-through. We must learn from those failures. The financial implications have been carefully assessed. While the initial investment is significant, the long-term benefits substantially outweigh the costs. Economic analysis demonstrates positive returns across multiple metrics. Job creation, improved service delivery, and enhanced public confidence all flow from getting this right. The alternative is continued deterioration and escalating costs down the road. International comparisons provide valuable lessons. Other jurisdictions have confronted similar challenges and developed effective solutions. We should adapt their best practices to our context rather than reinventing the wheel. Evidence-based policymaking demands that we examine what works elsewhere and apply those insights intelligently. Stakeholder consultation has been extensive. Industry representatives, community groups, professional associations, and individual citizens have all contributed their perspectives. The synthesis of that input has informed the current proposal. No policy will satisfy everyone, but this represents a balanced approach that addresses the most critical concerns while remaining fiscally responsible. The timeline for implementation must be realistic. Overpromising and underdelivering erodes public trust. Better to set achievable targets and exceed them than to announce ambitious plans that collapse under scrutiny. I urge the Minister to provide concrete commitments on key milestones and to report regularly on progress against those benchmarks.

We cannot afford delays that compound existing problems. The constituents I represent have made their views abundantly clear through correspondence and public meetings. They expect action, not excuses. They expect accountability, not bureaucratic deflection. This House must respond to those legitimate expectations with concrete measures. I have reviewed the relevant departmental briefings and consulted with experts in the field. The technical aspects are complex but manageable with proper planning. What we need is political will to drive implementation forward. Previous attempts have faltered due to inadequate coordination and insufficient follow-through. We must learn from those failures. The financial implications have been carefully assessed. While the initial investment is significant, the long-term benefits substantially outweigh the costs. Economic analysis demonstrates positive returns across multiple metrics. Job creation, improved service delivery, and enhanced public confidence all flow from getting this right. The alternative is continued deterioration and escalating costs down the road. International comparisons provide valuable lessons. Other jurisdictions have confronted similar challenges and developed effective solutions. We should adapt their best practices to our context rather than reinventing the wheel. Evidence-based policymaking demands that we examine what works elsewhere and apply those insights intelligently. Stakeholder consultation has been extensive. Industry representatives, community groups, professional associations, and individual citizens have all contributed their perspectives. The synthesis of that input has informed the current proposal. No policy will satisfy everyone, but this represents a balanced approach that addresses the most critical concerns while remaining fiscally responsible. The timeline for implementation must be realistic. Overpromising and underdelivering erodes public trust. Better to set achievable targets and exceed them than to announce ambitious plans that collapse under scrutiny. I urge the Minister to provide concrete commitments on key milestones and to report regularly on progress against those benchmarks.
